chapter.name: Cell: The Building Block of Life
chapter.blurb: Cells are introduced as the basic structural and functional unit of life, studied through microscopes given the eye's limit of resolution. The chapter builds up a working cell from its selectively permeable membrane and osmosis, through the rigid cell wall and the prokaryotic/eukaryotic divide, into the nucleus and genetic material, the ribosome-ER-Golgi-lysosome production and clean-up pathway, mitochondria and plastids for energy and food, and the vacuole for storage -- before turning to how cells divide (mitosis and meiosis) and to the classical Cell Theory and a cell's controlled life and death, including cancer, programmed cell death and totipotency.

scope_in.item: Explain why a microscope is needed to study cells, using the eye's limit of resolution (about 0.1 mm at the 25 cm near point) and magnification by a convex lens or combination of lenses

State that Robert Hooke first observed and named cells in 1665 while examining cork, and use a light microscope's total magnification (eyepiece x objective) to estimate a cell's real size from the field-of-view diameter and cell count (Activity 2.1)
Describe an electron microscope's use for finer, nanometre-scale detail beyond a light microscope
Describe the cell membrane's structure (fluid-mosaic model: lipid bilayer with embedded proteins) and its selective permeability
Define diffusion and osmosis, and distinguish isotonic, hypotonic and hypertonic solutions, using the potato, onion peel and cheek cell experiments
Describe the cell wall's structure (made mainly of cellulose), its permeability, and its role in keeping plant cells firm and shaped, contrasted with animal cells which lack it

State the three basic parts of a cell (plasma membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus) and distinguish prokaryotic cells (no defined nucleus/organelles, e.g. bacteria) from eukaryotic cells (plant and animal), including typical cell diameter and the cytoskeleton
Describe the nucleus's structure (nuclear membrane, pores, nucleolus) and the relationship between chromatin, chromosomes, DNA and genes as carriers of genetic information
State that mature red blood cells lack a nucleus and so cannot repair or divide, and that J. Craig Venter's 2010 synthetic-DNA experiment showed DNA controls a cell's structure and activities
Describe ribosomes, the endoplasmic reticulum (rough and smooth), the Golgi apparatus and lysosomes, and their roles in making, processing, packaging and disposing of cell materials
Describe mitochondria's structure (outer membrane, cristae) and role in cellular respiration and ATP production
Describe plastids -- chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts -- and their roles in photosynthesis, colour and food storage
Describe the vacuole's role in storing water, minerals, sugars and waste, and maintaining a plant cell's firmness

Describe cell division as the source of growth, repair and reproduction, and distinguish mitosis (identical daughter cells, growth/repair/asexual reproduction) from meiosis (four daughter cells with half the chromosome number, formed in reproductive organs for sexual reproduction), including the consequences of errors in each
Describe cell culture as growing cells outside the body in controlled, sterile, nutrient-rich conditions, and its uses
State the classical Cell Theory and the scientists behind it (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow)
Describe how normal cells grow, divide and die in a controlled way, including contact inhibition, cancer, and Programmed Cell Death
Describe totipotency, as proposed by Haberlandt, and its link to Plant Tissue Culture Technology

scope_out.reason: Presented in a 'Ready to Go Beyond' enrichment box (p.15); these are explicitly acellular (not made of cells), so they fall outside this chapter's subject, which is the structure of cells.

concepts.name: Studying cells: resolution and magnification
concepts.description: Why cells need microscopes to be seen and studied; limit of resolution, magnification, and the tools used.
concepts.idea: Cells are usually smaller than the eye's limit of resolution, so we need microscopes that magnify and resolve them clearly.
concepts.rule: The unaided human eye can distinguish two points only if they are about 0.1 mm apart when viewed from the near point (25 cm) -- this is called the limit of resolution. Since most cells are smaller than this, a convex lens or a combination of lenses (objective + eyepiece) is used to magnify them. Robert Hooke first observed cells in 1665 using a self-designed microscope (200-300X) while examining cork, and named them 'cells'. School light microscopes use different objective lenses (10X, 40X) for magnification and resolution; total magnification = eyepiece magnifying power x objective magnifying power. Electron microscopes use a beam of electrons instead of light, letting scientists see cell structures at the nanometre scale, far beyond what light microscopes reveal.
concepts.example: A microscope with a 10X eyepiece and 10X objective gives 100X total magnification, so a 200 micrometre onion cell appears 100 times larger under it.

questions.q: Explain why Robert Hooke could see 'cells' in cork but modern scientists needed electron microscopes to see finer cell structures like ribosomes.
questions.a: Hooke's microscope (about 200-300X) could resolve cell-sized compartments in cork, but structures like ribosomes are far smaller than a cell and need the far higher resolution of an electron microscope, which works at the nanometre scale, to be seen clearly.

questions.q: A student says 'a microscope with higher magnification always shows a cell more clearly.' Evaluate this statement using the ideas of magnification and resolution.

Resolution is the ability to see two close points as separate; without enough resolution, magnifying further does not add clarity

Reason: cork is dead plant tissue, so he saw the cell walls/empty compartments, not living cell contents

s: Method: measure field of view diameter, place the new sample, count cells across the diameter
Convert measurements to consistent units (mm to micrometres)
Formula: estimated cell size = field diameter (micrometres) divided by number of cells counted

concepts.name: Cell membrane: selective permeability, diffusion and osmosis
concepts.description: The cell membrane's structure and its role in controlling what enters and leaves the cell, including diffusion and osmosis.
concepts.idea: The cell membrane is a thin, selectively permeable boundary built of a lipid bilayer with embedded proteins (the fluid-mosaic model), which lets water move by osmosis toward the region with less water.
concepts.rule: The cell membrane (plasma membrane) surrounds and protects the cell, and is selectively permeable -- it allows some substances through while blocking others. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration (with or without a membrane). Osmosis is specifically the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane, from a region with more water (dilute/hypotonic solution) to a region with less water (concentrated/hypertonic solution), until concentrations equalise (isotonic). Structurally the membrane is about 7-10 nanometres thick, made of a lipid bilayer (water-attracting heads out, water-repelling tails in) with proteins embedded and free to move -- hence 'fluid' -- arranged like tiles in a mosaic, hence 'fluid-mosaic model'. Proteins act as gatekeepers controlling what passes through.
concepts.example: A potato piece placed in plain water swells (water moves in by osmosis, since water is greater outside than the solute concentration); the same piece placed in concentrated salt or sugar solution shrinks (water moves out).

questions.q: A student places two identical potato pieces, one in distilled water and one in a strong salt solution, and weighs each before and after one hour. Explain the results she should expect, and why.

questions.q: Two cheek cell slides are prepared; one is placed in a 20 per cent sugar solution and one is left in water. After 30 minutes, one has shrunk considerably and one looks unchanged. Which is which, and why?
questions.a: The slide in 20 per cent sugar solution has shrunk considerably, because the hypertonic solution draws water out of the cells by osmosis; the one left in water looks largely unchanged since there is little net movement of water.

questions.q: Onion peel cells and cheek cells are both placed in a concentrated sugar solution. The onion cells' boundary stays the same size while their inner content shrinks; the cheek cells shrink considerably overall. Explain this difference.

Cheek cells have no cell wall, so when they lose water the entire cell shrinks.
s: Onion (plant) cells have a rigid cell wall outside the cell membrane

questions.a: Yes, this is sound. Plain water is dilute (hypotonic) compared with the cell contents, so water moves into the plant cells by osmosis, restoring their water content and firmness; a sugar solution would instead be hypertonic and draw water out, making wilting worse.
s: Judgement: yes, it is sound

Expected result if osmosis applies the same way: cells in salt solution show membrane pulling away from the wall (shrunk contents), cells in water stay plump

concepts.name: Cell wall; prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
concepts.description: The rigid outer covering found in plant, fungal and bacterial cells, and the structural difference between cells with and without a well-defined nucleus.
concepts.idea: A cell wall gives rigidity to plant, fungal and bacterial cells; cells are classed as prokaryotic (no defined nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles) or eukaryotic (defined nucleus, membrane-bound organelles) based on this organisation.
concepts.rule: In addition to the cell membrane, plant, fungal and bacterial cells have a rigid but permeable outer cell wall -- made mainly of cellulose in plants -- that lets water and dissolved minerals pass, helps plant roots absorb water, and keeps cells and plant parts firm and upright, even though animal cells (which have no cell wall) can change shape freely. Every cell has three basic parts: a selectively permeable plasma membrane, a semi-fluid cytoplasm, and (usually) a prominent nucleus; the cytoplasm holds organelles, mostly visible only under an electron microscope. A bacterial cell has no well-defined nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles -- its genetic material sits in a region called the nucleoid -- so it is called prokaryotic (pro = primitive, karyon = nucleus). Plant and animal cells have a well-defined, membrane-bound nucleus and several membrane-bound organelles, so they are called eukaryotic (eu = true). Eukaryotic cells (10-100 micrometres) are typically larger than prokaryotic cells (1-10 micrometres), and eukaryotic cells also have a fine fibre network called the cytoskeleton that gives structural support and helps movement.
concepts.example: An onion peel cell (plant, eukaryotic, has a wall) stays box-shaped and regular, while a human cheek cell (animal, eukaryotic, no wall) is irregularly shaped.

s: Plant cell: well-defined, membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles (eukaryotic)

questions.q: Explain why animal cells (which have no cell wall) can change shape easily, while plant cells generally cannot, and relate this to the roles each cell type plays in the organism.
questions.a: Animal cells are bounded only by the flexible cell membrane, without a rigid cell wall, so they can change shape easily -- this flexibility supports the movement of animal tissues (such as muscle or blood cells). concepts.name: Nucleus and genetic material
concepts.description: The nucleus, its parts, and how chromosomes, chromatin, DNA and genes carry a cell's hereditary information.
concepts.idea: The nucleus is the eukaryotic cell's control centre, holding DNA that carries genetic information -- visible as thread-like chromatin in a resting cell and as rod-shaped chromosomes when the cell is dividing.
concepts.rule: The nucleus has a double-layered nuclear membrane with pores that let material pass between nucleus and cytoplasm; inside it, the nucleolus is a dense round body where ribosomal subunits are made before moving to the cytoplasm to form ribosomes. The nucleus contains chromosomes -- rod-shaped structures visible only when the cell is about to divide, made of DNA and specific proteins. DNA molecules carry the genetic information; the functional segments of DNA are called genes. In a non-dividing cell, this DNA exists as chromatin, an entangled thread-like mass, which organises into chromosomes only when the cell is about to divide. Prokaryotic cells have no such nucleus; their DNA is a single circular molecule with associated proteins in a region called the nucleoid. Some specialised cells, like mature human red blood cells, lose their nucleus entirely (enucleate) and so cannot repair or divide, giving them a short lifespan. In 2010, J. Craig Venter's team showed that DNA controls a cell's structure and activities, by inserting synthetic DNA copied from one bacterium (Mycoplasma mycoides) into another bacterium's emptied cell, which then grew and divided following the synthetic DNA's instructions.
concepts.example: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus, which frees up space for haemoglobin but also means they cannot divide and survive only about 120 days.

questions.q: A student argues that red blood cells are 'incomplete' or 'less important' because they lack a nucleus. Do you agree? Justify your answer.

questions.q: Design a simple classroom demonstration (using a model or diagram) to show a classmate the difference between chromatin and a chromosome, and explain what each part of your model represents.

Explain to the classmate that both models are made of the same 'DNA' (the wool) -- only how tightly it is organised changes, depending on whether the cell is dividing.
s: Model idea: e.g. a loosely tangled length of string/wool to represent chromatin
Model idea: the same string neatly coiled/folded into a short rod shape to represent a chromosome
Explanation: both represent the same DNA, just in different states -- chromatin in a non-dividing cell, chromosome in a dividing cell

concepts.name: Ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus and lysosomes
concepts.description: The organelles that make, process, package and dispose of a cell's proteins and other materials.
concepts.idea: Proteins are made by ribosomes, processed and transported through the endoplasmic reticulum, packaged by the Golgi apparatus, and unwanted material is broken down by lysosomes -- a coordinated production-and-clean-up pathway.
concepts.rule: Ribosomes, found free in the cytoplasm or attached to the endoplasmic reticulum, are the sites of protein synthesis. The Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER) is a large, network-like organelle continuous with the nuclear membrane, involved in synthesis and transport of proteins, lipids and some hormones; Rough ER (RER) has ribosomes attached and looks rough, mainly making and secreting proteins (e.g. in pancreatic gland cells), while Smooth ER (SER) has no ribosomes, looks smooth, and is involved in synthesising and storing fats and hormones. The Golgi apparatus is a stack of flattened, sac-like structures, functionally linked to the ER and cell membrane; it acts like the cell's post office, modifying, sorting and packaging proteins and lipids into vesicles for transport, secretion or lysosome formation -- first observed in 1898 by Camillo Golgi in barn owl nerve cells. Lysosomes are single membrane-bound sacs filled with enzymes that break down unwanted proteins, carbohydrates, fats and damaged cell parts, keeping the cell clean; the breakdown products are released into the cytoplasm for reuse. In human fertilisation, lysosomal enzymes in the sperm help break down the outer layer of the egg.
concepts.example: In pancreatic gland cells, which secrete large amounts of digestive enzymes (proteins), the rough ER -- with its many attached ribosomes -- is especially well developed.

questions.q: Ribosomes are the site of

questions.a: Golgi apparatus

questions.q: Explain how Camillo Golgi's discovery of the Golgi apparatus illustrates how scientific ideas can be doubted before later being confirmed.
questions.a: Golgi first observed a thread-like network in nerve cells in 1898 using special staining techniques, but early microscopes could not resolve it clearly, so many scientists doubted the structure existed. Only decades later, when electron microscopes became available, was the structure clearly confirmed -- after which it was named the Golgi apparatus in his honour, showing how scientific claims can wait for better tools before being accepted.
s: Golgi observed a thread-like network using special staining in 1898
Early microscopes could not resolve it clearly, so many doubted its existence
Electron microscope observations decades later confirmed the structure, which was then named in his honour

questions.q: Consider: (I) Ribosomes are found only attached to the endoplasmic reticulum. (II) Lysosomes release breakdown products into the cytoplasm, where they may be reused. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only II

questions.q: A cell that secretes large amounts of hormones made of fat is found to have very little Rough ER but a lot of Smooth ER. Explain why this makes functional sense.
questions.a: This makes sense because Smooth ER is the organelle involved in synthesising and storing fats and hormones, which is exactly what this cell specialises in; since it does not need to make and secrete large amounts of protein, it has little need for Rough ER.
s: SER is involved in synthesis and storage of fats and hormones
RER is mainly for protein synthesis/secretion, which this cell does not need much of, so it needs relatively little RER

questions.q: Explain why the ER, Golgi apparatus and lysosomes are described as functionally linked, using the journey of a protein destined for secretion.
questions.a: A protein made by ribosomes on the ER is processed and transported through the ER's network, which is functionally linked to the Golgi apparatus. The Golgi then modifies, sorts and packages the protein into vesicles, which may be secreted out of the cell, sent to the cell membrane, or become a lysosome -- showing that the ER, Golgi apparatus and lysosomes work together as one coordinated production-and-delivery pathway rather than as isolated parts.

The Golgi apparatus, functionally linked to the ER, modifies, sorts and packages the protein into vesicles
Depending on the vesicle's destination, it may be secreted, sent to the membrane, or become a lysosome -- showing the organelles work as one coordinated pathway

questions.q: A student says lysosomes are 'harmful' to the cell because they contain powerful enzymes that can break down proteins and fats. Do you agree? Justify your answer.
questions.a: Disagree -- lysosomal enzymes are kept safely contained within the lysosome's own membrane and are used in a controlled way to break down only unwanted proteins, carbohydrates, fats and damaged organelles, which keeps the cell clean and healthy rather than harming it.
s: Judgement: disagree
Reason: lysosomal enzymes are normally contained within the membrane-bound sac and only break down unwanted/damaged material in a controlled way, keeping the cell clean and healthy

questions.q: Design a simple flow diagram (describe the boxes and arrows) showing how a digestive enzyme protein moves from being made to being released from a pancreatic cell.
questions.a: Draw boxes in order: Ribosome on the Rough ER (synthesises the protein) to Rough ER (processes and transports it) to Golgi apparatus (modifies, sorts and packages it into a vesicle) to vesicle moving to the cell membrane to secretion outside the cell. Arrows connect each box in this order, each labelled with the step's role -- synthesis, processing, packaging, and release.
s: Boxes: Ribosome (on RER) to RER to Golgi apparatus to vesicle to cell membrane/secretion
Arrows showing the correct order of movement between these organelles
Labels explaining each step's role (synthesis, processing/transport, packaging, release)

concepts.name: Mitochondria, plastids and vacuoles
concepts.description: The organelles that supply energy, make and store food, and store water and other materials in a cell.
concepts.idea: Mitochondria release energy from food as ATP through cellular respiration; plastids (chloroplasts, chromoplasts, leucoplasts) make or store plant food and pigments; vacuoles store water, minerals, sugars and waste and keep plant cells firm.
concepts.rule: Mitochondria, the 'powerhouse of the cell', are surrounded by two membranes -- a smooth, porous outer membrane and an inner membrane folded into cristae that increase surface area for chemical reactions; in mitochondria, glucose and other molecules are broken down during cellular respiration, releasing energy stored as ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate), the cell's energy currency. Plants use plastids for food synthesis and storage: chloroplasts are double-membrane-bound organelles containing the green pigment chlorophyll in disc-shaped structures within a semi-fluid stroma, which absorbs light energy for photosynthesis, with the resulting sugars and starch stored in the stroma. Chromoplasts contain non-green pigments (yellow, orange, red) that colour flowers and fruits, attracting pollinators and seed-dispersing animals. Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food such as starch (e.g. potato, taro), oils or proteins. Mitochondria and plastids both have their own DNA and ribosomes and can make some of their own proteins, suggesting an evolutionary link to single-celled organisms. A mature plant cell usually has one large central vacuole, bounded by a selectively permeable membrane and filled with cell sap, storing water, minerals, sugars and waste; by holding water it keeps the cell firm (turgid), and a plant wilts when its vacuoles lose water. Animal cells may have smaller vacuoles for temporary storage.
concepts.example: A potato's leucoplasts store starch, which is why potato cells turn blue-black with iodine, while a ripe tomato's chromoplasts give it its red colour.

questions.a: powerhouse of the cell

questions.q: Compare the roles of mitochondria and vacuoles in a plant cell.
questions.a: Mitochondria release energy from glucose and other molecules through cellular respiration, storing it as ATP for the cell's activities. Vacuoles instead store water, minerals, sugars and waste, and by holding water they keep the plant cell firm (turgid).
s: Mitochondria: break down glucose/molecules to release energy as ATP (cellular respiration)
Vacuoles: store water, minerals, sugars and waste, and keep the cell firm through water pressure

questions.q: A plant is kept without water for several days and its leaves droop, but when watered again it recovers within hours. Explain this using the role of the vacuole, and why the recovery is possible.
questions.a: Without water, the plant cells' vacuoles lose water and the cells become less firm, so the leaves droop. Because the cell membrane and wall are not damaged -- only the water content of the vacuole has dropped -- watering the plant again lets the vacuoles take up water by osmosis, restoring internal pressure and firmness, so the plant recovers.
s: Without water, the vacuoles lose water and the cells become less firm, causing wilting/drooping

When watered, the vacuoles take up water again by osmosis, restoring pressure inside the cells and making the plant firm again

questions.q: A student argues that leucoplasts are 'less important' than chloroplasts because they cannot make food through photosynthesis. Do you agree? Justify your answer.
questions.a: Disagree -- leucoplasts do not make food, but they perform the equally essential role of storing food such as starch, oils or proteins for the plant's later use, a function chloroplasts are not specialised for; both are important in their own roles.
s: Judgement: disagree (a reasoned answer either way is acceptable if justified)
Reason: leucoplasts perform an equally essential role in storing food (starch, oils, proteins) for later use, which chloroplasts do not do

questions.q: Design a simple experiment (like the iodine test) that a student could use to find out whether a food-storing plant part, such as a potato, stores its food mainly as starch in leucoplasts or as sugar in vacuoles.
questions.a: Cut a thin slice of the plant part and add a few drops of iodine solution: a blue-black colour shows starch is present, which in a food-storing part is typically stored in leucoplasts. To check for sugar, taste a fresh slice or use a simple sugar test on the squeezed juice; sweetness without a strong iodine colour suggests the food is mainly stored as dissolved sugar in the vacuole's cell sap rather than as starch.
s: Method: cut a thin slice, apply iodine solution to test for starch (blue-black colour indicates starch)
Compare with a control or a different test (e.g. taste, or a sugar test) for dissolved sugar in cell sap/vacuole
Conclusion rule: a strong blue-black colour with iodine points to starch stored in leucoplasts; sweetness without the colour points to sugar mainly stored in the vacuole's cell sap

concepts.name: Cell division: mitosis and meiosis
concepts.description: How new cells are formed from existing cells for growth, repair and reproduction, through mitosis and meiosis.
concepts.idea: Cells divide by mitosis to grow and repair the body with genetically identical cells, and by meiosis to form gametes with half the chromosome number for sexual reproduction.
concepts.rule: Cell division is the process by which new cells are formed from pre-existing cells, allowing organisms to grow, repair damaged tissue and reproduce; eukaryotic cells divide in a controlled, orderly manner through the cell cycle. There are two major types: mitosis, the most common type, produces two genetically identical daughter cells from one parent cell, each with the same DNA and chromosome number as the parent -- important for normal growth, repair, maintenance and asexual reproduction. Meiosis occurs only in the cells of reproductive organs (testes and ovaries in animals; anthers and ovaries in plants) and produces gametes; the parent cell divides twice in succession to form four daughter cells, each with half the chromosome number of the parent, restoring the original number when two gametes combine at fertilisation -- this creates genetic variation, which is why children resemble but are not identical to their parents. Errors in mitosis can cause uncontrolled cell division and tumours or an abnormal number of chromosomes in body cells; errors in meiosis may cause genetic disorders, developmental problems, or reduced fertility/early pregnancy loss. Scientists can also grow cells outside the body in a nutrient-rich medium under sterile, controlled conditions -- a technique called cell culture, used to study cells and produce biochemicals, food, medicines and vaccines.
concepts.example: A cut on the skin heals because skin cells divide by mitosis to replace the damaged ones, producing new cells genetically identical to the originals.

questions.a: Body cells such as skin or muscle cells divide by mitosis because it produces genetically identical daughter cells with the full, normal chromosome number, which is what growth and repair of body tissue needs; meiosis halves the chromosome number and only occurs in reproductive organs to form gametes, which would be inappropriate for ordinary body cells.

questions.q: A doctor observes that a patient's body cells are dividing uncontrollably, forming a tumour, while another patient has a child with a genetic disorder linked to a parent's reproductive cells. Identify which type of cell division error is most likely responsible in each case, and explain your reasoning.
questions.a: The tumour is most likely caused by an error in mitosis, since errors in mitosis lead to uncontrolled division of body cells and can produce tumours or abnormal chromosome numbers in those cells. The child's genetic disorder is most likely linked to an error in meiosis, since meiosis forms the gametes, and errors there can cause genetic disorders passed to offspring.
s: Tumour in body cells: error in mitosis (uncontrolled division of body cells)
Genetic disorder from reproductive cells: error in meiosis (affecting gametes)
Reasoning: mitosis errors cause uncontrolled division/abnormal chromosome numbers in body cells (tumours); meiosis errors affect gamete formation, causing inherited genetic disorders

questions.q: Consider: (I) Mitosis is important for asexual reproduction. (II) Meiosis creates genetic variation among offspring. Which is or are correct?

questions.q: Explain why children resemble their parents but are not exactly identical to them, using the idea of meiosis.

s: Meiosis produces gametes with variation, since each gamete gets a different half-set of chromosomes
A child's chromosomes come from combining gametes from both parents at fertilisation, giving a unique but related combination

questions.q: The chapter asks: if skin cells started dividing by meiosis instead of mitosis, what would happen to a cut on the skin? Answer this, explaining your reasoning.
questions.a: If skin cells divided by meiosis instead of mitosis, the new cells produced would have only half the normal chromosome number and would not be genetically identical to the original skin cells, since meiosis is meant to form gametes, not replacement body cells. As a result, the cut would not heal properly, because normal wound repair depends on mitosis producing identical cells with the full chromosome number.
s: Meiosis produces gametes with half the chromosome number, not identical body cells
New skin cells formed this way would have the wrong (halved) chromosome number and would not be genetically identical/functional replacements
The cut would not heal properly, since normal skin repair depends on mitosis producing identical, fully-chromosomed replacement cells

questions.q: A student claims that cell culture 'replaces' the need to study mitosis and meiosis in a living organism. Do you agree? Justify your answer.
questions.a: Disagree -- cell culture is simply a laboratory tool that lets scientists grow and study cells (including how they divide) outside the body under controlled conditions; it does not replace mitosis and meiosis, which are the actual processes of cell division happening inside living organisms.
s: Judgement: disagree

Reason: cell culture is a tool that lets scientists study cell division and other cell activities more easily outside the body, but the processes of mitosis and meiosis themselves still occur inside living organisms and are not replaced by the technique

questions.q: Design a simple comparison chart (describe its structure) that a student could use to quickly tell whether a described cell division event is mitosis or meiosis.
questions.a: Make a chart with two columns, Mitosis and Meiosis, and rows for features such as number of divisions (one vs two), number of daughter cells (two vs four), chromosome number in daughter cells (same as parent vs half of parent), where it occurs (most body cells vs only reproductive organs), and purpose (growth/repair/asexual reproduction vs forming gametes for sexual reproduction). A student can match a described event's features row by row to decide whether it is mitosis or meiosis.
s: Structure: two columns headed Mitosis and Meiosis
Rows for key features: number of divisions, number of daughter cells, chromosome number in daughter cells, where it occurs, purpose
Use: match the described event's features against each row to identify mitosis or meiosis

concepts.name: Cell theory and the cell life cycle
concepts.description: The classical Cell Theory and how cells are controlled in their growth, division and eventual death.
concepts.idea: The Cell Theory states that all living things are made of cells, the cell is life's basic unit, and all cells come from pre-existing cells; cells also grow, divide and die in a controlled way, and losing that control causes problems like cancer.
concepts.rule: Matthias Schleiden (1838) showed all plants are made of cells, Theodor Schwann (1839) showed all animals are made of cells, and Rudolf Virchow (1855) showed that new cells form only from pre-existing cells -- together giving the classical Cell Theory: all living organisms are made of one or more cells; the cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living beings; and all cells arise from pre-existing cells. Cells grow and divide in a controlled way, stay in the right place, carry out their functions, and eventually die when no longer needed, with dead cells replaced by new ones; in many animal cells, division normally stops once cells contact their neighbours, a process called contact inhibition, but plant cells, with their rigid walls, do not show contact inhibition. Cancer cells lose this control and keep dividing uncontrollably, forming tumours that (if malignant) can invade nearby tissue and spread elsewhere in the body. Cells also have a genetically regulated process of controlled self-destruction called Programmed Cell Death (PCD), essential for normal development (for example, eliminating cells between developing fingers in an embryo so hands are not webbed). In 1902, Austrian botanist Gottlieb Haberlandt proposed that a plant cell, even a mature one, retains the ability to develop into a complete plant given suitable nutrients and conditions -- a property called totipotency, which laid the foundation for Plant Tissue Culture Technology.
concepts.example: Without Programmed Cell Death removing the cells between an embryo's developing digits, human hands would form webbed rather than separated fingers.

questions.a: Theodor Schwann

questions.q: According to the classical Cell Theory, new cells arise
questions.a: only from pre-existing cells

questions.q: The process by which many animal cells stop dividing once they come into contact with neighbouring cells is called ____.
questions.a: contact inhibition

questions.a: all cells contain chlorophyll

the cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living beings
all cells arise from pre-existing cells

o: lose control over cell division and keep dividing uncontrollably

questions.a: a mature plant cell to develop into a complete plant given suitable conditions
o: a mature plant cell to develop into a complete plant given suitable conditions

questions.q: Explain why plant cells do not show contact inhibition, unlike many animal cells.
questions.a: Many animal cells stop dividing once they touch their neighbours (contact inhibition), but plant cells, due to their rigid cell walls, grow differently and do not show this same contact-based stopping of division.
s: Plant cells have rigid cell walls
This rigid wall means plant cells follow a different pattern of growth and do not stop dividing simply upon contact with neighbours, unlike many animal cells

questions.q: Gottlieb Haberlandt's idea of totipotency laid the foundation for
questions.a: Plant Tissue Culture Technology
o: the discovery of the Golgi apparatus

questions.q: A human embryo's fingers separate from each other during development mainly because of
questions.a: Programmed Cell Death removing the cells between the digits
o: Programmed Cell Death removing the cells between the digits
mitosis stopping completely in the hand

questions.q: A tumour that invades nearby tissue and spreads to other parts of the body is described as
questions.a: malignant

questions.q: A researcher observes an unusual mass of tissue that keeps growing without stopping, even though the cells around it are fully grown. Using the ideas in this chapter, suggest what is likely happening and why.
questions.a: This is likely a tumour formed by cancer cells, which have lost the normal control over cell growth and division -- such as contact inhibition -- that keeps normal cells from dividing once they are fully grown and in contact with their neighbours.
s: Likely a tumour caused by cancer cells
Reason: cancer cells lose the normal control over cell growth/division (such as contact inhibition) and keep dividing uncontrollably

questions.q: Haberlandt's totipotency experiments are best supported by later plant tissue culture work in which
questions.a: a single plant cell grown in suitable nutrients develops into a whole new plant
o: a single plant cell grown in suitable nutrients develops into a whole new plant
an animal cell divides by meiosis to form gametes
a chloroplast is isolated from a leaf cell

questions.q: According to the Cell Theory, a newly discovered single-celled organism found on another planet would still be expected to
questions.a: be made of at least one cell, with the cell as its basic unit of structure and function
o: be made of at least one cell, with the cell as its basic unit of structure and function
form only by spontaneous generation from non-living matter

questions.q: Explain, using the ideas of contact inhibition and cancer, why a small skin wound normally heals and then stops growing new tissue, but a cancerous growth does not stop.
questions.a: A healing wound's skin cells divide by mitosis to replace the lost tissue, but normally stop dividing once the gap is filled and the cells come into contact with their neighbours -- contact inhibition. Cancer cells have lost this control, so even when surrounded by other cells they keep dividing uncontrollably, which is why a cancerous growth keeps expanding instead of stopping like a healed wound.
s: Healing: skin cells divide by mitosis to replace lost cells, and normally stop once the wound is repaired and cells contact their neighbours (contact inhibition)
Cancer: cancer cells have lost this contact-inhibition control
Result: cancer cells keep dividing uncontrollably even when surrounded by other cells, forming a growing tumour instead of stopping

questions.q: Assertion (A): Cancer cells form tumours that can invade nearby tissue and spread to other parts of the body. Reason (R): Cancer cells have lost the normal control (such as contact inhibition) that stops cell division once a task is complete.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Explain how Programmed Cell Death (PCD) and cancer represent opposite failures of the same underlying control system.
questions.a: PCD is the normal, genetically regulated process by which cells are selectively destroyed when the body needs it, part of a controlled balance between cell growth and death. Cancer represents the opposite kind of failure -- cells lose control over division and multiply uncontrollably instead of stopping or dying appropriately -- showing that both too much uncontrolled growth (cancer) and disrupted controlled death are problems within the same overall control system.
s: PCD is a normal, controlled process where cells are destroyed in an organised way when needed
Cancer is a loss of the normal control over cell division, causing uncontrolled growth instead of the usual balance of growth and controlled death

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: 'Since all cells arise from pre-existing cells, a completely new type of cell can never be created in a laboratory.' Use evidence from the chapter to support or challenge this claim.
questions.a: The evidence in the chapter broadly supports this claim so far: even in Venter's synthetic biology experiment, only the DNA was made synthetically -- the rest of the cell (cytoplasm, membrane) came from an already-living cell -- and Haberlandt's totipotency and modern plant tissue culture also grow new cells and plants starting from an existing living cell, not from non-living matter. So while science has learned to control and direct cells in powerful new ways, a completely new cell built entirely from scratch, with no pre-existing cell involved, has not yet been achieved, consistent with the Cell Theory principle.
s: Cell Theory states cells only arise from pre-existing cells, which held true even in Venter's synthetic DNA experiment (the recipient cell's cytoplasm/membrane were from an existing cell)
Haberlandt's totipotency and tissue culture also show new plants/cells growing from an existing cell, not from nothing

Conclusion: the claim is broadly supported by the evidence so far -- no fully synthetic cell built entirely from non-living matter has been created; DNA and tissue culture techniques still start from a pre-existing living cell

questions.q: A student argues that plants cannot get cancer because they do not show contact inhibition. Evaluate this claim using the chapter's content.
questions.a: This claim goes beyond what the chapter actually states. The chapter only says plant cells, due to their rigid walls, do not show contact inhibition and follow a different growth pattern -- it does not claim this makes plants immune to cancer-like uncontrolled cell growth. Without more evidence, the claim that plants 'cannot' get cancer is not fully supported by the chapter.
s: Judgement: the claim is questionable / not directly supported

Reason: the chapter only states plant cells don't show contact inhibition and grow differently; it does not say this makes them immune to cancer-like uncontrolled growth, and a reasoned answer should note the chapter does not give enough evidence either way

questions.q: Design a short poster (describe its sections and key message) to explain to younger students why controlled cell division matters, using both a healthy example (wound healing) and a failure example (cancer).
questions.a: The poster could have two main sections: one showing a healing skin wound, explaining that mitosis replaces the damaged cells and then stops through contact inhibition once the wound is repaired; and a second section showing a tumour, explaining that cancer cells have lost this control and keep dividing without stopping, letting the growth spread. The key message running through both: cell division is essential, but it must be carefully controlled -- start when needed, and stop when the job is done -- for the body to stay healthy.
s: Section 1: what controlled cell division normally does -- mitosis replaces damaged/dead cells (e.g. wound healing) and stops via contact inhibition once repair is complete
Section 2: what happens when control is lost -- cancer cells divide uncontrollably, forming tumours that can spread
Key message: cell division must be controlled (growth, then stopping) to keep the body healthy
